S8. RQ4: The registered mediation analyses and additional analyses

November 18, 2026
Emma Marshall, J.D., M.A.
University of Nebraska-Lincoln

Notes shared by tables of this section.

  • Tables 1-S8.1, 1-S8.2, 1-S8.5, 1-S8.7, 1-S8.10, 1-S8.13 and 1-S8.16: Intervals: two-sided 95% percentile bootstrap intervals (type 6) from participant resamples stratified within the six conditions, 10,000 attempted and 10,000 usable.
  • Tables 1-S8.1, 1-S8.2 and 1-S8.5: No attitude was missing, so no values were imputed.
  • Tables 1-S8.1 and 1-S8.2: A letter is supported when its interval lies on the predicted side of zero.
  • Tables 1-S8.1 to 1-S8.3 and 1-S8.5: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence.
  • Tables 1-S8.1 to 1-S8.3 and 1-S8.5 to 1-S8.18: n per condition, primary sample: Illegal abortion: No information 68, Expected evidence 63, Unexpected evidence 63; Improper disposal: No information 71, Expected evidence 66, Unexpected evidence 67 (all 398 in the analysis).
  • Tables 1-S8.2 and 1-S8.3: Confidence in the chosen ruling is rated on the 0–100 scale; differences are in scale points.
  • Tables 1-S8.7, 1-S8.8, 1-S8.12, 1-S8.13, 1-S8.15 and 1-S8.16: A letter is supported in a legal context when its interval lies on the predicted side of zero.
  • Tables 1-S8.7 to 1-S8.18: Expected evidence = evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion; unexpected evidence = financial-crime evidence; each is contrasted with no information.
  • Tables 1-S8.8 and 1-S8.13: Indirect effects are products of the unstandardized paths of their route, in probit units of the ruling per outcome contrast; the abortion-minus-disposal rows are differences of those products.
  • Tables 1-S8.8 and 1-S8.13: The run reports no global fit for a model with a probit endpoint (the registration names none).
  • Tables 1-S8.9 and 1-S8.14: Ruling paths are in probit units (latent-response residual variance = 1); other paths are unstandardized in their original units.
  • Tables 1-S8.9 and 1-S8.14: WLSMV: robust standard errors, two-sided normal Wald 95% intervals, and two-sided p values.
  • Tables 1-S8.10 and 1-S8.16: Indirect effects are in confidence points (0–100 scale) per outcome contrast.
  • Tables 1-S8.17 and 1-S8.18: Joint 95% percentile bootstrap bands (type 6) for each comparison’s two curves used 10,000 participant resamples within the six conditions (9,983 usable).
  • Tables 1-S8.17 and 1-S8.18: Reported without a verdict (no registered decision rule).

Figure 1-S8.1

Predicted probability of finding probable cause after each kind of outcome information, by legal context

Note. I used the primary-sample probit model to predict each participant’s probable cause ruling in every condition, retaining that participant’s attitudes. The points average these marginaleffects predictions. The bars give two-sided 95% delta-method intervals based on the model’s robust covariance. The intervals are symmetric on the probability scale and can extend beyond its limits. The registered comparisons and their percentile bootstrap intervals are in the tables. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Predicted = the registered sign of the difference; the legal-context comparisons have no registered direction and are reported without a verdict. Figure 1-S8.2

Predicted probability of finding probable cause across each judgment in the joint model, by legal context and outcome information

Note. Predicted probabilities of a probable cause ruling from the joint probit model with the attitudes in the primary sample. I varied one judgment across its observed range in each panel, holding the other four judgments and four attitudes at the means of all participants in the model. Evidence relevance is the observed ten-item mean. I evaluated predictions on a fixed grid and used the robust covariance to obtain two-sided 95% delta-method bands, truncating the symmetric probability-scale intervals at 0 and 1. The table above reports the slopes with percentile bootstrap intervals. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Figure 1-S8.3

Fitted hypothesized chains of the registered serial model (H4b–H4d)

Note. H4b and H4c trace expected and unexpected evidence through evidence relevance and pregnancy-evidence likelihood to scalar probable cause confidence. H4d is the difference between these indirect effects. The registered primary-sample model uses the ten-item mean for relevance. I retained the H1 route through consequence severity to foreseeability. Path labels give unstandardized estimates in the original units, with robust (Huber–White) Wald 95% intervals. The paths from outcome information to each mediator and from likelihood to the outcome have separate estimates for illegal abortion and improper disposal, labeled Abortion and Disposal. Both contexts share the relevance-to-likelihood and severity-to-foreseeability estimates. Solid lines indicate intervals excluding zero; dashed lines indicate intervals including it. I dash a path with two estimates only when both intervals include zero. The path table gives the omitted direct paths from outcome information to likelihood, foreseeability, and the outcome, the foreseeability-to-outcome path, attitude slopes, and disturbance covariances. The indirect-effect table gives the products of the paths. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Figure 1-S8.4

Fitted relevance chain of the probable-cause ruling (E12a–E12c)

Note. E12a and E12b trace expected and unexpected evidence through evidence relevance and pregnancy-evidence likelihood to the probable cause ruling. E12c is the difference between these indirect effects. I show these pathways from the fitted registered model with the four attitudes in the primary sample. Path labels give unstandardized estimates in the original units, with the ruling’s endpoint path in probit units. The coefficient table gives registered percentile bootstrap intervals for the paths into the ruling. The path table gives robust Wald intervals for every path. The paths from outcome information to relevance and from likelihood to the ruling have separate estimates for illegal abortion and improper disposal, labeled Abortion and Disposal. Both contexts share the relevance-to-likelihood estimate. I draw every path as a solid line. I omit the severity route, direct paths, attitude slopes, and disturbance covariances. The path table gives the direct paths. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Figure 1-S8.5

Fitted relevance and severity chains of confidence in the ruling (E12d)

Note. The figure shows the fitted registered model with the four attitudes in the primary sample. E12d covers two chains. One runs from the evidence to evidence relevance, then to pregnancy-evidence likelihood, and then to confidence in the ruling. The other runs from the evidence to consequence severity, then to foreseeability, and then to confidence. Each path shows its unstandardized estimate and robust (Huber–White) Wald 95% interval in the original units. The paths from the evidence to each mediator and the paths into confidence are estimated in each legal context and show both estimates, labeled Abortion (illegal abortion) and Disposal (improper disposal). The path from relevance to likelihood and the path from severity to foreseeability are the same in both contexts. Solid paths have intervals that exclude zero, and dashed paths have intervals that include zero. A path with two estimates is dashed only when both intervals include zero. The figure omits the direct paths, the attitude slopes, and the disturbance covariances. The path table reports the direct paths. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Fitted two-mediator chains of the probable-cause ruling (E13a–E13h)

Note. Fitted parallel mediation model of outcome information and the probable cause ruling in the primary sample, with likelihood and foreseeability as mediators and the four attitudes as covariates. The likelihood and foreseeability coefficients on the ruling are E13a and E13b. Indirect effects of expected and unexpected evidence through likelihood are E13c and E13d; for unexpected evidence, the indirect effect through foreseeability is E13e and the sum across both mediators is E13f. E13g and E13h are the direct effects of outcome information. Unstandardized estimates are shown separately for illegal abortion (Abortion) and improper disposal (Disposal). Estimates for paths into the ruling are in probit units; all others are in their original units. All paths are solid. The coefficient table reports registered percentile bootstrap intervals for every path, and the path table reports robust Wald intervals. The path table also includes the unlettered expected-evidence path to foreseeability, attitude slopes, and mediator-disturbance covariance omitted from the diagram. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

Figure 1-S8.7

Fitted two-mediator chains of confidence in the ruling (E13i–E13p)

Note. Fitted parallel mediation model of outcome information and confidence in the ruling in the primary sample, with likelihood and foreseeability as mediators and the four attitudes as covariates. The likelihood and foreseeability coefficients on confidence are E13i and E13j. Indirect effects of expected and unexpected evidence through likelihood are E13k and E13l; for unexpected evidence, the indirect effect through foreseeability is E13m and the sum across both mediators is E13n. E13o and E13p are the direct effects of outcome information. Each path has an unstandardized estimate and robust (Huber–White) Wald 95% interval in the original units for illegal abortion (Abortion) and improper disposal (Disposal). Solid lines indicate that an interval excludes zero in at least one legal context; dashed lines indicate that both intervals include zero. The path table reports the unlettered expected-evidence path to foreseeability, attitude slopes, and mediator-disturbance covariance, which are omitted from the diagram. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.

The paths of the two-mediator model of confidence are printed elsewhere, cell for cell: its likelihood and foreseeability equations and their disturbance covariance in Table 1-S7.17, and its confidence equation in Table 1-S8.11. None of its paths is equal across the legal contexts.

Figure 1-S8.8

Average predicted probability of finding probable cause across the likelihood rating, by condition, one panel per legal context

Note. Predicted probability of finding probable cause by likelihood rating and outcome condition, from the registered threshold model with the four attitudes in the primary sample. I averaged predictions over participants within each legal context at each outcome-by-likelihood combination. The dashed .50 line identifies the threshold probability, and an open circle marks the likelihood rating where a curve crosses it. Shading gives pointwise 95% delta-method intervals from the robust covariance, cut at 0 and 1. I used the registered joint band to obtain the threshold sets in the tables; the shaded pointwise intervals do not define those sets. Expected evidence is evidence consistent with a self-managed abortion. Unexpected evidence is evidence of a financial crime. Each is compared with no information. Primary sample n per condition: illegal abortion, 68 with no information, 63 with expected evidence, and 63 with unexpected evidence; improper disposal, 71 with no information, 66 with expected evidence, and 67 with unexpected evidence. All 398 participants are in the analysis.
